28925:
Daniel was a young man of Judah's nobility deported to Babylon in the first wave of exiles. Trained in Babylonian learning and renamed Belteshazzar, he rose to high office under Nebuchadnezzar and continued in public life into the Persian period. The first half of his book (chapters 1-6) tells stories of faithfulness at a foreign court: refusing the king's food, interpreting dreams, reading the writing on the wall, and surviving the lions' den. In each, God vindicates those who refuse to compromise and humbles proud kings.

The second half (chapters 7-12) records Daniel's own visions: four beasts and a son of man given an everlasting kingdom, a ram and goat, seventy 'weeks' of years, and a long revelation of conflicts culminating in resurrection. These apocalyptic chapters shaped Jewish and Christian hope; Jesus called himself the Son of Man and spoke of 'the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet' (Matt 24:15).

The date of the book is among the most debated questions in Old Testament study. Traditional readers take it as written by Daniel in the sixth century BC, with genuine predictive prophecy. Most critical scholars date its final form to about 167-164 BC, during the persecution by Antiochus IV, with the visions functioning as history written as prophecy up to that crisis. Many others hold intermediate views, with older court tales collected and the visions added later.
28926: Daniel was taken in the third year of Jehoiakim (Dan 1:1-6), served the king until Cyrus's first year (Dan 1:21), and received a vision in Cyrus's third year (Dan 10:1). He was set over the wise men of Babylon (Dan 2:48), served Belshazzar as third ruler (Dan 5:29) and Darius as one of three chief officials (Dan 6:2). He prayed three times a day toward Jerusalem (Dan 6:10). Ezekiel names a Daniel with Noah and Job as a model of righteousness and wisdom (Ezek 14:14; Ezek 14:20; Ezek 28:3). Jesus refers to 'Daniel the prophet' (Matt 24:15), and Hebrews alludes to those who stopped the mouths of lions (Heb 11:33).
28927: Daniel is placed among the Writings rather than the Prophets in the Hebrew Bible, and the Talmud does not count him a prophet in the same sense (b. Megillah 3a), though he was greater in wisdom. His fidelity to dietary law and prayer became a model for diaspora Jews; the seventy weeks have been read as ending with the destruction of the Second Temple.
28928: Daniel is one of the four major prophets. Their Bibles include the Greek additions: the Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men in chapter 3, and the stories of Susanna and Bel and the Dragon. The stone cut without hands (Dan 2:34) was read by the Fathers as Christ born of the Virgin, and the son of man (Dan 7:13) as Christ.
28930: Sixth-century authorship is defended on grounds of Jesus' attribution, fragments of Daniel at Qumran close to the proposed Maccabean date, the accurate portrait of Belshazzar as co-regent, and the possibility of predictive prophecy. The seventy weeks are often calculated to reach Jesus' ministry and death. Dispensationalists separate the seventieth week as a future tribulation; others see it fulfilled in Christ's first coming.
28931: Most date the final book to c. 167-164 BC: chapter 11 tracks Hellenistic history in detail up to Antiochus IV's persecution but is inaccurate about his death, suggesting composition before 164 BC. Problems cited include Darius the Mede, unknown outside Daniel, and Belshazzar called Nebuchadnezzar's son. Defenders reply that 'son' can mean successor and that Darius may be a title for Gubaru or for Cyrus himself (reading Dan 6:28 as 'Darius, that is, Cyrus').

29001: Nebuchadnezzar II ruled the Neo-Babylonian Empire from 605 to 562 BC, the most powerful king of his age. He crushed Egypt at Carchemish, deported Judah's elite in 597 BC, and destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's temple in 586 BC. Jeremiah calls him the LORD's servant, an instrument of judgment (Jer 25:9; Jer 27:6), while Daniel depicts a proud king brought to confess that the Most High rules the kingdom of men.

Others note that Babylonian sources for Nebuchadnezzar's later reign are sparse.

29066:
Esther (Hadassah) was a Jewish orphan of the tribe of Benjamin, raised in Susa by her cousin Mordecai, who became queen to the Persian king Ahasuerus, usually identified with Xerxes I (486-465 BC). When the royal official Haman secured an empire-wide decree to annihilate the Jews, Mordecai urged her to intervene. After a three-day fast she approached the king uninvited at the risk of her life, outmanoeuvred Haman through two banquets, and obtained a counter-decree that allowed her people to defend themselves.

The book named for her is famous for never mentioning God by name, though fasting, providential 'coincidences' (a sleepless king, a reversal of fortunes) and Mordecai's hint that deliverance would arise 'from another place' point to hidden divine action. It explains the origin of Purim, the festival of lots, and Esther herself issues a written decree confirming it.

Esther has been read as a model of courage, of faithful presence within a foreign power, and of a woman's decisive leadership. Questions about the book's historicity and about its Greek form, which adds explicit prayers and mentions of God, have made it one of the most discussed books of the canon.
29067: She is daughter of Abihail, Mordecai's uncle, and was adopted by Mordecai (Esth 2:7; Esth 2:15). She was made queen in the seventh year of Ahasuerus (Esth 2:16-17), concealed her identity (Esth 2:10), risked death to approach the king (Esth 4:11-16), exposed Haman (Esth 7:3-6), and wrote with full authority to confirm Purim (Esth 9:29-32). The Hebrew text never names God.
29068: The Megillah is read publicly at Purim with noisemakers drowning Haman's name. Rabbinic tradition sees God's hiddenness (hester panim) wordplayed in her name and counts her among seven prophetesses (b. Megillah 14a). Some sages discussed whether she was blameless in marrying a gentile king, concluding she acted under compulsion.
29069: Their canon includes the Greek additions (some 107 verses): Mordecai's dream, the text of the royal decrees, and prayers of Mordecai and Esther that make God's role explicit. Esther interceding before the king is read as a figure of Mary interceding for the faithful.
29070: The Hebrew book alone is canonical. It is valued as a study in providence, where God works through ordinary events without miracle. Luther voiced strong reservations about the book; most Protestant traditions have nonetheless embraced it as Scripture.
29071: Many scholars read Esther as a historical novella or diaspora court tale, citing Herodotus' statement that Xerxes' queen was Amestris, the improbable scale of the events, and the absence of Esther in Persian records. Others defend a historical core, noting accurate details of Persian court life and the attestation of an official named Marduka at Susa in the Persepolis tablets.
